chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Sovereign Debt Actually Is

lessons.title: Who Lends to Governments: G-Secs, Eurobonds, and Multilateral Loans

children.text: The last lesson looked at why governments borrow. This one looks at who is actually on the other side of that transaction, handing over the money. The answer changes almost everything about how risky that borrowing is. A rupee borrowed from an Indian bank that is required by law to hold government bonds behaves nothing like a dollar borrowed from a foreign investor who can sell out in seconds. Same government, same use of funds, very different risk.
The Domestic Market: Where Most of India's Borrowing Happens

markDefs.definition: The minimum share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (deposits) that it must hold in specified liquid assets, mostly government bonds. Currently set at 18% by the RBI.

children.text: Well over 95% of India's government debt is raised at home, in rupees, from Indian lenders. The single biggest buyer is the domestic banking system, which holds government securities (G-Secs) partly because it wants safe, liquid assets, and partly because it has to. Under the

, every bank must park a fixed share of its deposits in government bonds and similar instruments. That single rule creates a large, dependable pool of demand for G-Secs before the market even opens each morning.

Insurance companies and pension and provident funds are the next big buyers, for a similar reason: regulation requires LIC, EPFO, and pension funds to hold a large share of their assets in government or government-guaranteed bonds, since these funds are managing long-term liabilities, like your eventual pension, and need matching long-term, low-default-risk assets. The RBI itself holds a meaningful chunk of G-Secs too, though it acquires them mainly through Open Market Operations to manage liquidity and interest rates, not to directly fund the deficit, a distinction covered in the previous lesson.

body.text: Notice how much of this demand is captive rather than purely market-driven. Banks, insurers, and pension funds are not always buying G-Secs because they think it's the best possible return, they are buying because regulation requires it. That captive demand is one reason the Indian government has historically been able to borrow large amounts at home without a genuine debt crisis: a big chunk of its lenders cannot simply walk away, unlike a foreign bondholder deciding whether to roll over a maturing Eurobond.

children.text: Borrowing Abroad: Why India Mostly Avoids Foreign-Currency Bonds

markDefs.definition: A term coined by economists Barry Eichengreen and Ricardo Hausmann for the inability of most emerging market governments to borrow internationally in their own currency, forcing them into foreign-currency debt and the exchange rate risk that comes with it.

children.text: is simply a bond a government issues in a foreign currency, usually US dollars, sold mostly to foreign investors. This is where currency risk enters the picture. If the government of, say, Sri Lanka borrows in dollars but earns its revenue in rupees, a sharp fall in the rupee makes every dollar of debt more expensive to repay overnight, with no change in how much was actually borrowed. Economists call this trap
: most emerging markets simply cannot convince foreign investors to lend in their own currency in size, so they borrow in dollars or euros instead and absorb the currency risk themselves.

India has, so far, mostly opted out of this trap for its own government borrowing. The central government has never issued a sovereign dollar bond. In the July 2019 Budget, the Finance Ministry did propose a modest programme of external sovereign borrowing in foreign currency, partly to diversify funding sources and ease pressure on domestic bond yields. The plan drew sharp criticism from economists and former RBI governors, who flagged exactly the currency mismatch risk described above, and it was largely shelved. India's general government external debt today is small, only around 3-4% of GDP, a sharp fall from levels near 19% of GDP around the 1991 balance of payments crisis, and it remains almost entirely on concessional or semi-concessional terms from multilateral and bilateral lenders rather than commercial market debt.

columns.label: Domestic-Currency Debt (e.g. Rupee G-Secs)
points: No currency mismatch: revenue and debt are in the same currency
A weaker rupee does not directly increase the debt burden
Backed partly by captive, regulation-driven domestic demand
Can, in extreme cases, be inflated away, at a real cost to savers

columns.label: Foreign-Currency Debt (e.g. Sovereign Eurobonds)
points: Currency mismatch: a weaker local currency directly raises the real debt burden
Usually needed when domestic savings are too small to fund large deficits
Investor base is more flighty and rate-sensitive than captive domestic buyers
Often carries lower headline interest rates, which is precisely the temptation

children.text: Multilateral and Bilateral Lending: Cheaper Money With Strings Attached

A third category sits between fully domestic borrowing and a commercial foreign bond: loans from multilateral institutions like the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), and bilateral loans from other governments, most visibly Japan through JICA. These loans are almost always tied to specific projects, a metro line, a rural water scheme, a highway corridor, and typically carry interest rates well below what the same government would pay in the open market, sometimes with repayment periods stretching past 30 years.

The Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project is a well-known example: JICA is funding roughly 80% of the project cost through a loan carrying an interest rate near 0.1%, repayable over 50 years with a long moratorium before repayment even begins. That is a very different animal from a Eurobond priced off where the market thinks India's credit risk sits that week. The trade-off is that multilateral and bilateral loans sometimes come with conditions attached: procurement rules, environmental and social safeguards, or, in the case of IMF programmes covered later in this course, explicit policy reforms as a condition of disbursement.

body.title: Two Countries, Two Lender Mixes
body.scenario: Country A raises 90% of its government debt domestically in its own currency, mostly from regulated banks and pension funds required to hold it. Country B raises 60% of its government debt through dollar-denominated Eurobonds sold to foreign fund managers, because its domestic savings pool is too small to fund its deficit.
body.prompt: If both countries' currencies fall 20% against the dollar in a single year, which country's debt burden is affected more, and through what mechanism?
body.modelAnswer: Country B is hit far harder. Its debt is denominated in dollars while its revenue is collected in its own currency, so a 20% currency depreciation makes the local-currency cost of repaying that dollar debt roughly 20% higher overnight, even though not a single new dollar was borrowed. Country A's debt is in its own currency, so a weaker currency does not mechanically increase what it owes domestic lenders. Country A still faces other risks from a currency fall, like imported inflation, but not this direct debt-servicing shock.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why does the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) matter for how India finances its fiscal deficit?
options: It sets the interest rate the government pays on G-Secs
It requires Indian banks to hold a fixed share of deposits in government bonds, creating steady, semi-captive domestic demand for that debt
It limits how much the government can borrow in a single year
It is the rate at which the RBI lends directly to the government
body.explanation: SLR is a reserve requirement on banks, currently 18% of net demand and time liabilities, that must be held in government securities and similar approved assets. It does not set bond yields or cap government borrowing directly, but by forcing a large, stable pool of demand into G-Secs, it makes it easier for the government to place a large borrowing programme domestically without depending entirely on foreign or purely voluntary buyers.

body.text: Who lends to a government, and in what currency, changes the risk of that debt as much as how much is borrowed. A rupee owed to a captive domestic bank is not the same liability as a dollar owed to a foreign bondholder who can sell out by lunchtime.

children.text: This lender mix is exactly why India's own sovereign risk looks quite different from countries like Sri Lanka, Zambia, or Ghana, which leaned heavily on commercial dollar borrowing and ran into exactly the currency mismatch problem described here. The next lesson turns to the raw numbers behind all of this: how debt-to-GDP, the external versus domestic split, and other metrics are actually put together, and why the mix, not just the headline ratio, is often what decides whether a country's debt load is manageable.

points: Over 95% of India's government debt is domestic, rupee-denominated, and bought mainly by banks, insurers, and pension funds, a large share of which are regulatory-driven, semi-captive buyers.

Foreign-currency sovereign debt, like a dollar Eurobond, creates a currency mismatch: a weaker local currency directly raises the real cost of repaying it, regardless of how much was originally borrowed.
'Original sin' describes the difficulty most emerging markets face in borrowing internationally in their own currency, pushing them toward foreign-currency debt and its risks.
India has never issued a sovereign dollar bond and keeps its general government external debt small, around 3-4% of GDP, almost entirely on concessional multilateral or bilateral terms.

Multilateral loans (World Bank, ADB, AIIB) and bilateral loans (like JICA) are typically project-tied and carry low interest rates and long tenors, but can come with procurement, safeguard, or policy conditions attached.

body.text: The holder shares, yield levels, and debt ratios in this lesson are approximate, drawn from recent RBI and government data, and will drift over time. Verify current figures against the RBI's Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy or its latest Public Debt Management Report before using them in analysis or advice.
